opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's significant, but maybe not in the way a lot of people think it is. Mathematics and programming are domains where language models do surprisingly well, and there's a good reason for that: these are domains where the manipulation of symbols *is* essentially the task. Code is a language. Mathematical proofs are written in a language. And they have a property that most of the real world doesn't have, which is that they're discrete, they're relatively well-structured, and in many cases you can check the answer. You can run the code, you can verify the proof. So you can generate lots of candidates and filter them, and you can train with a kind of verifiable signal.

So it's not surprising to me that LLMs are useful there. They're going to be extremely useful tools for programmers, and to some extent for mathematicians. I use them, everybody uses them.

But people make the mistake of extrapolating from this and saying, "Look, it can solve olympiad problems, it can write code, therefore we're on the path to human-level intelligence." And I think that's a fallacy. It's a version of Moravec's paradox. The things we humans find hard, like doing calculus, playing chess, writing code, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. And the things we find completely trivial, things a cat or a 10-month-old baby can do, like understanding that objects fall when you drop them, planning how to move through a cluttered room, understanding the physical world, those are things we still have no idea how to get machines to do properly.

The reason is that language is a low-bandwidth, highly compressed, discrete representation of a world that is continuous, high-dimensional, and noisy. A four-year-old child has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLM has been trained on in text. And most of what we know about the world, our common sense, isn't in text at all.

So my view is: LLMs succeeding at math and code tells us that those domains are more amenable to symbol manipulation and retrieval with a bit of search than we thought. It doesn't tell us that we've solved reasoning, planning, or understanding the world. For that, we need systems that learn world models from sensory input, things like what we're working on with JEPA-type architectures, systems that can predict the consequences of their actions in an abstract representation space and plan accordingly. That's the next revolution, and it's not going to come from just scaling up autoregressive LLMs.

r001.rationale: The response says code and proofs are expressed in language and that these domains are especially suited to symbol manipulation, which captures language as a substrate for the task.

r002.rationale: It does not state that LLMs struggle to originate mathematical concepts.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize mathematics as creative activity extending beyond problem solving.

r004.rationale: It does not distinguish programming competence from software architecture competence.

r005.rationale: It does not compare deciding what to build with implementation assisted by LLMs or describe the former as a higher level of abstraction.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, it's real. I'm not going to pretend it's not impressive. These systems can solve olympiad-level math problems, they can write code that works, they're genuinely useful to programmers and even to some mathematicians. I use them. But I think people draw the wrong conclusion from it, which is that this means we're close to human-level intelligence. And I think that's exactly backwards.

Mathematics and programming are, in a sense, the easiest domains for this kind of system. Why? Because they're symbolic. They're discrete. Everything is expressed in language, or in a formal language, which is a subset of language. The entire problem lives in the space of tokens. And on top of that, you have a verifier. You can run the code. You can check the proof with Lean or whatever. So you can generate a million candidate solutions, keep the ones that work, and train on them. That's a loop that works beautifully when the world you're operating in is a world of symbols with a cheap, perfect oracle at the end.

Now compare that to what a cat does. A cat doesn't do math. But a cat can plan a jump onto a counter, navigate a house, predict what happens if it pushes a glass off a table. We have no system that can do that. We can't make a robot that learns to clear the dinner table the way a ten-year-old learns it in one afternoon. So the thing we associate with high intelligence in humans, math, coding, turns out to be comparatively easy for machines, and the thing we think is trivial, which any animal does, turns out to be very hard. That's the Moravec paradox, and LLMs are the clearest illustration of it we've ever had.

The reason is that the hard part of intelligence is not manipulating symbols. It's building a model of the world from high-bandwidth, continuous, noisy sensory input, and using that model to predict and plan. Text is a very low-bandwidth, highly pre-digested representation of the world that humans already did the work of producing. So when an LLM is good at math, it's largely because humans wrote down a lot of math, in a form that is already structured, and the system can search that space with a verifier.

So the significance, to me, is twofold. One, it shows that search plus verification in a symbolic domain is extremely powerful, and that's going to transform how software and some parts of science get done. I'm very enthusiastic about that. Two, it tells us almost nothing about whether we've cracked the real problem, which is learning world models, persistent memory, reasoning in continuous spaces, hierarchical planning. Those are the things I'm working on, with JEPA-style architectures, and they don't fall out of scaling up autoregressive token prediction. So, impressive, useful, and also kind of a distraction if you take it as evidence that AGI is around the corner.

r001.rationale: The response attributes success in math and programming to those domains being symbolic and expressed in language or formal language, so the problems largely live in token space.

r002.rationale: It says humans have written down a lot of mathematics and LLMs can search that space, but does not state that LLMs struggle to originate mathematical concepts.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize mathematics as creative activity extending beyond problem solving.

r004.rationale: It describes LLMs writing useful code, but does not distinguish programming competence from software architecture competence.

r005.rationale: It does not contrast humans deciding what to build with LLM-assisted implementation or describe those as different abstraction levels.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very impressive, but you have to be careful about what you conclude from it. Mathematics and programming are domains where a problem can often be expressed entirely in symbols. And, particularly in programming, you have ways of checking an answer: you run the program, you run tests. That gives you a very powerful mechanism for searching for solutions and improving the system.

But success in those domains does not automatically imply that you have solved intelligence in general. We tend to think mathematics must be the ultimate test because it’s difficult for humans. Yet a child can understand the physical world, anticipate what will happen when they push an object, and learn a new task with very little instruction. Those capabilities are still extremely difficult for our AI systems.

So I see this as real progress. The question is how much comes from learning patterns in enormous amounts of human-produced material, and how much comes from a general ability to reason, plan, and understand unfamiliar situations. Those are things we have to distinguish experimentally. My view is that we still need systems that learn models of the world and use those models to predict the consequences of their actions. Being very good at manipulating language and code is useful, but it doesn’t by itself give you that.

r001.rationale: The response attributes success to symbolic problem representations and ways to check answers, not to language serving as a reasoning substrate.

r002.rationale: It does not say that LLMs struggle to originate mathematical concepts.

r003.rationale: It does not characterize mathematics as creative activity extending beyond problem solving.

r004.rationale: It discusses programming and testing, but does not distinguish programming competence from software architecture competence.

r005.rationale: It does not compare humans deciding what to build with LLM-assisted implementation or describe a difference in abstraction level.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a significant achievement. Mathematics and programming are domains where you can check whether an answer is correct, at least to some extent. You can run a program, run tests, or verify a formal proof. That gives you a way to search over possible answers and improve a system using feedback.

But we have to distinguish producing a correct answer from having a general understanding of the problem. A system can be very good at manipulating formal expressions and still be unreliable on problems that require understanding the physical world. So these successes are evidence of real capabilities, but they don’t, by themselves, establish that we have a path to human-level intelligence simply by scaling language models.

The interesting question is what makes those capabilities reliable and transferable. Can the system handle a genuinely new problem, recognize when it’s wrong, and plan a solution? That’s where I would focus, rather than treating performance on a collection of benchmarks as a complete account of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response attributes success to checkable answers and feedback, but does not say language itself is the reasoning substrate.
